title: An LLM that can only veto my crypto trades, never size them — 20yo solo project, looking for people who've actually built something like this
author: Burnerphone_13

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: Does the veto apply only to new crypto entries, or can the LLM also block an exit? Even without sizing authority, blocking an exit could extend exposure beyond what the underlying strategy intended. I'd make protective exits independent of the model and explicitly define what happens when a veto request times out. A useful test case is an entry awaiting an LLM response when an existing position hits its stop: does that exit still go through immediately?

replies.author: Burnerphone_13
replies.body:
Good point. In the current design, the LLM veto applies only to new entries. Claude is called through the planned  confirm_trade_entry()  integration, so exits are not routed through the gatekeeper.   

Existing positions remain under the quantitative strategy and risk controls. Protective exits must be independent of the LLM, and a stop or other risk exit must never wait for an LLM response.

The fail-safe rule for an entry is explicit: if the LLM call times out, errors, or returns malformed/truncated output, the entry is rejected. It must never default to approval. That failure must not block an exit.

Therefore, the test case you describe should behave as follows:
A new entry is waiting for the LLM response.

An existing position hits its stop or protective exit.

The exit is sent immediately through the independent Freqtrade/exchange path.

If the LLM request later times out, only the pending entry is rejected; the exit is unaffected.

One important caveat: the Freqtrade wiring is not fully implemented and validated yet, so this is the intended architectural contract, not a claim that the integration has already been proven in production. I’ll make this an explicit integration test before paper trading.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the 5 minute instead of daily run is a rite of passage, I don't know anyone who has built one of these without one in their past.

the thing I'd flag on the gatekeeper is that you can't really backtest it. replaying Claude's verdict over two years of Donchian signals is slow, costs money and isn't deterministic, so your clean backtest is going to be Freqtrade alone, and the veto's effect stays unmeasured right up until paper. so make paper do that job: log every veto with the model's stated reason, and keep tracking the vetoed trade as if it had been taken. after a month you can put approved and vetoed side by side and see whether the gate is removing bad trades or just removing trades.

I built Quantradin to run that exact loop, though on US equities and options rather than crypto: an agent writes the rule, the engine grades it without look-ahead, and a shadow desk keeps score of what the rule would have done. there's no charge and everything it trades is paper, so if the equities side is ever useful you can find it through my posts.

replies.author: Burnerphone_13
replies.body:
Ha, good to know the 5-minute mistake is a rite of passage. It stung less once I knew that.

Your point about the gatekeeper is the one I needed to hear. I'd been half-assuming I could measure the veto in backtest, and you're right that it isn't practical: too slow, too costly, and non-deterministic on top. So the clean backtest will be Freqtrade alone, and paper has to do the job of measuring the gate.

Logging every veto with the model's stated reason and tracking the vetoed trade as if it had been taken is exactly the comparison I want. I'll pin the model and prompt version for the whole paper phase so approved vs. vetoed stays comparable. With daily signals across a small universe I expect the sample to be thin, so I'll wait for a meaningful number of signals rather than a fixed month.

One question if you don't mind: did you see veto rates drift when the model version changed, or was that stable enough not to worry about?

Thanks for the Quantradin mention too. I'll keep it in mind if I ever look at equities.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: log the vetoes with the model's reason from day one, because a month from now the only way to know if the gate earns its keep is the trades it said no to. the approved ones tell you nothing on their own.
